raw_response:
I am 68 this year, been farming these fields since I was thirteen. My father taught me everything I know. I only finished primary school, but I know my land better than any book. I have 8 mu total, just me and my wife working it now. Six mu I do wheat then maize — that's how we eat and pay for daily costs. Two mu I plant cotton for cash money, though picking it gets harder on my back every year.

For the wheat, I will plant the same improved variety my neighbor Lao Zhang used last year — he got over 900 jin per mu, so I bought seed from him. I rotary till the ground in October like always. Before planting I put down one full bag of compound fertilizer per mu, that's 50 jin. Then when the wheat turns green in March, I topdress with another 25 jin of urea per mu. I know fertilizer is expensive this year, but my nephew tried saving money last year and used less — his wheat went yellow and thin. I will not take that risk. Better to spend the money than lose the crop. I irrigate three times: once before the freeze so the wheat survives winter, once at green-up, and once at heading if the rain doesn't come. The pump costs electricity, but dry wheat is worthless. I spray twice for aphids and rust.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I have no time to waste. I plant hybrid maize seed right away — no-tillage, just open the row and put the seed in. Some people rotary till between crops but I don't have time or energy for that, and the maize grows fine if I plant deep enough. I put compound fertilizer in the planting hole, about half a bag per mu, and when the maize is knee-high I topdress with urea. I figure about 30 jin of urea total per mu for the maize. I irrigate once in summer if the rains don't come — usually they do, but I have the well if I need it. Two sprays for the corn borer.

The cotton on my two mu takes more fussing. I rotary till in April and plant an improved variety, not the fancy hybrid seeds that cost too much. I put down compound fertilizer before planting, a bit less than one bag per mu, and topdress again when it flowers. Cotton needs water at flowering and when the bolls are forming, so two irrigations. But the real trouble is the bugs — bollworm, aphids, mites. I have to spray four times or the worms will eat everything. I expect about 260 jin of seed cotton per mu. It's less land than grain, but the price per jin is better, and the cotton cash pays for my medicine and the pump electricity.

I thought about cutting back on everything because costs went up, but at my age I can't afford a bad year. If I lose half my wheat, I don't have another way to make it up. I will do what I did last year, maybe a tiny bit more fertilizer to be safe.
